newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks funds for Russian space programme.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks funds for Russian space programme.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, tackling a host of problems after a long holiday, gave the green light on Friday for raising $100 million in foreign credits for Russia's beleagured space programme.

He also reassured Russians that lopping three zeroes off the rouble would not cause anyone to suffer and, trying to ease tensions in the North Caucasus, told the leaders of two volatile regions to make peace or lose his backing.

Touring the Khrunichev space centre in Moscow as a new crew on the space station Mir was briefed on their mission to repair the damaged craft, Yeltsin said Russia was on target to complete its part in building an international space station.

"All problems in building the Russian part of the station have been solved, including financial questions. The construction is going according to schedule," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.

Yeltsin, who returned to Moscow on Tuesday after a month's vacation, signed a decree permitting the finance ministry to raise $99.5 million from foreign banks to fund Russia's involvement in building the Alpha space station.
The new funds are intended to ensure the government can carry out promises to provide enough additional funds to ensure Russia can complete its contruction projects for Alpha on time.

Its ability to do so had been in question since it completed the first of Alpha's 36 planned modules months behind schedule, causing concern among its partners -- the United States, the European Space Agency, Japan, Canada and Italy.

The difficulties of Russia's space programme, which is struggling for cash, have been highlighted by a string of problems on Mir since a module attached to the station was punctured during a docking manoeuvre on June 25.

The relief crew, Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov, docked with Mir on Thursday and began a week-long briefing on Friday. They are due to start risky repairs on August 20 to try to fix the station's damaged power supply.
Yeltsin, 66, has had a busy schedule since his return to Moscow and set about solving a number of pressing problems.

He has tried to mend fences with the patriarch of Russia's Orthodox Church after differences over a proposed law on religious minorities and arranged a meeting next week with the president of breakaway Chechnya.
He also met the head of the natural gas monopoly Gazprom to signal his approval of the influential company's work.

Yeltsin preceded his return by announcing a denomination of the national currency under which one new rouble will equal 1,000 old ones from January 1. He dedicated his regular radio address on Friday to easing Russians' fears about the reform.

"Of course previous reforms, starting from 1947, always took something from citizens...As a result there was panic, stress, people crushed in lines and always victims," Yeltsin said. "Nothing like that will happen now."
"With this currency reform we declare firmly that we have conquered inflation. We have it firmly under control," he said.

Yeltsin also met the leaders of North Ossetia and Ingushetia on Friday after a rise in tensions in their North Caucasus regions bordering breakaway Chechnya. The Kremlin fears a new conflict over a long-running territorial dispute between them.
"I want you to end this undeclared war between you today, once and for all," RIA news agency quoted him as saying.
It said he had told them they would not get his support when they face re-election next year unless they toe the line.
